title: Practical techniques and uncertainties; Concentration and standard solutions; Tests for ions
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for CCEA A-level Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: PR01b#t3 term and clue written for the game; PR01b#t4 term and clue written for the game; AM03#t1 term and clue written for the game; AM03#t3 term and clue written for the game. Questions: AM03#N.3a, PR01b#N.9, PT07#N.3, AM03#N.7, PT07#N.6, AM03#N.9, PT07#N.12, AM03#N.11, PT07#N.14a.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Risk
items.clue: The chance of harm, given how a substance is used.

items.label: Independent variable
items.clue: The one factor you deliberately change in an investigation.

items.label: Concentration
items.clue: Amount of solute divided by the volume of the whole solution.

items.label: Volumetric flask
items.clue: Glassware filled until the bottom of the meniscus sits on the mark.

questions.stem: What amount of sodium hydroxide is present in 25.0 cm³ of NaOH(aq) in which [NaOH] = 0.100 mol dm⁻³?

options.text: 2.50 mol

questions.stem: A student must heat a reaction mixture containing ethanol (highly flammable, boiling point 78 °C) for 30 minutes. Which plan best controls the risk?

options.text: Heat it over a Bunsen burner on a low flame, in a fume cupboard.
Heat it over a Bunsen burner, wearing gloves and eye protection.
Heat it under reflux, using a water bath or an electric heater.
Heat it in an open beaker so that the vapour can escape.

questions.explanation: No naked flame, and the condenser returns ethanol vapour to the flask, so little escapes.

questions.stem: Which result shows that a solid contains ammonium ions?

options.text: Dilute hydrochloric acid is added; a gas forms that turns limewater milky.
It is warmed with NaOH(aq); a gas forms that turns damp red litmus paper blue.
NaOH(aq) is added to its solution; a white precipitate forms that stays on warming.
Its solution turns damp blue litmus paper red, and no gas forms on warming.

questions.explanation: OH⁻ ions remove H⁺ from NH₄⁺, releasing ammonia, the only common alkaline gas.

questions.stem: A student prepares 100.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol dm⁻³ CuSO₄(aq) by placing 3.19 g of CuSO₄(s) in a 100.0 cm³ volumetric flask, dissolving it in some distilled water, adding distilled water to the mark and mixing. The concentration is later found to be less than 0.200 mol dm⁻³. Which of the following could explain this result?

options.text: The flask still held some distilled water from rinsing when the CuSO₄ was added.
Water was added until the bottom of the meniscus was above the mark.
Half of the solution was poured into a beaker before its concentration was measured.
The CuSO₄ dissolved completely, so no solid could be seen in the flask.

questions.explanation: Overfilling makes the volume more than 100.0 while the amount stays 0.0200 mol, so c = n/V falls.

questions.stem: A student adds barium chloride solution to a solution of an unknown sodium salt, without adding acid first. A white precipitate forms. Why can the student not yet conclude that sulfate ions are present?

options.text: Barium chloride gives a white precipitate with every negative ion.
The white solid could be sodium chloride crystallising out of the mixture.
The solid could be barium carbonate, which acid would have prevented.
Barium ions react with water to form a white barium hydroxide precipitate.

questions.explanation: BaCO₃ is also white and insoluble. Dilute HCl first removes carbonate as CO₂, so a white precipitate after acidifying must be BaSO₄.

questions.stem: A student adds 600.0 cm³ of water to 200.0 cm³ of 0.500 mol dm⁻³ NaCl(aq), giving 800.0 cm³ of solution. What is the concentration of NaCl in the diluted solution, in mol dm⁻³?
A white solid gives a brick-red flame. Its solution fizzes with dilute hydrochloric acid, giving a gas that turns limewater milky. What is the solid?

options.text: Calcium carbonate
Lithium carbonate
Calcium sulfate
Sodium carbonate

questions.explanation: Brick-red is Ca²⁺; fizzing with a gas that turns limewater milky is CO₃²⁻.

questions.stem: Seawater contains about 1.29 g of magnesium ions, Mg²⁺, per dm³. How many moles of Mg²⁺ are in 250 cm³ of seawater? Data: Ar Mg 24.3.

options.text: 13.3 mol

questions.stem: A garden-centre sack of white fertiliser crystals has lost its label. It could be ammonium sulfate, ammonium carbonate, ammonium chloride or potassium sulfate. Which pair of results shows it is ammonium sulfate?

options.text: Warming with NaOH(aq) gives a gas that turns damp red litmus blue; BaCl₂(aq) gives a white precipitate that fizzes and dissolves when dilute HCl is added.
Warming with NaOH(aq) gives no alkaline gas; dilute HCl then BaCl₂(aq) gives a white precipitate.
Warming with NaOH(aq) gives a gas that turns damp red litmus blue; dilute HCl then BaCl₂(aq) gives a white precipitate.
Warming with NaOH(aq) gives a gas that turns damp red litmus blue; dilute HNO₃ then AgNO₃(aq) gives a white precipitate.
